fetched_contents.text: Natural Polymer-Based Hydrogels: From Polymer to Biomedical Applications Abstract Hydrogels prepared from natural polymer have attracted extensive attention in biomedical fields such as drug delivery, wound healing, and regenerative medicine due to their good biocompatibility, degradability, and flexibility. This review outlines the commonly used natural polymer in hydrogel preparation, including cellulose, chitosan, collagen/gelatin, alginate, hyaluronic acid, starch, guar gum, agarose, and dextran. The polymeric structure and process/synthesis of natural polymers are illustrated, and natural polymer-based hydrogels including the hydrogel formation and properties are elaborated. Subsequently, the biomedical applications of hydrogels based on natural polymer in drug delivery, tissue regeneration, wound healing, and other biomedical fields are summarized. Finally, the future perspectives of natural polymers and hydrogels based on them are discussed. For natural polymers, novel technologies such as enzymatic and biological methods have been developed to improve their structural properties, and the development of new natural-based polymers or natural polymer derivatives with high performance is still very important and challenging. For natural polymer-based hydrogels, novel hydrogel materials, like double-network hydrogel, multifunctional composite hydrogels, and hydrogel microrobots have been designed to meet the advanced requirements in biomedical applications, and new strategies such as dual-cross-linking, microfluidic chip, micropatterning, and 3D/4D bioprinting have been explored to fabricate advanced hydrogel materials with designed properties for biomedical applications. Overall, natural polymeric hydrogels have attracted increasing interest in biomedical applications, and the development of novel natural polymer-based materials and new strategies/methods for hydrogel fabrication are highly desirable and still challenging. Keywords: hydrogel, natural polymer, drug delivery, tissue engineering, wound healing 1. Introduction Hydrogels are three-dimensional networks formed by hydrophilic polymers through chemical cross-linking (covalent bond, ionic bond) or physical cross-linking (hydrogen bond, van der Waals force, physical entanglement). They can swell in water and retain a certain shape while absorbing a large quantity of water, attracting increased interest in numerous areas since they were first reported by Wichterle and Lim in the 1960s [1]. Natural polymers, which are formed from photosynthesis or a biochemical reaction in the natural world or extracted from natural products, are ideal skeletons for the fabrication of hydrogels because of their diversified properties such as their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and environmental friendliness. Hydrogels based on natural polymers such as alginate, starch, cellulose, chitosan, gelatin, collagen, hyaluronic acid, and so on show a good degradability, biocompatibility, nontoxic degradation products, a good flexibility similar to natural tissue, and are in natural abundance [2], which endow them with widespread applications in medicinal fields, for instance, as carriers for drug delivery, wound dressing for wound healing, substrates for cell culture, scaffolds for tissue regeneration, and so on [3,4]. Biocompatibility is one of the most significant characteristics of hydrogels for biomedical application, referring to the ability of a material to contact with bodily organs with minimum damage to the surrounding tissues and without triggering undesirable immune responses but performing its desired function in a medical treatment [5]. Hydrogels based on natural polymers usually have excellent biocompatibility owing to the intrinsic properties of natural polymers. However, for most of the natural polymeric hydrogels, their limited toughness and poor mechanical properties become major obstacles to their application. Several efforts were made to improve the mechanical properties of hydrogels, including chemical cross-linking, physical cross-linking and mixing with other synthetic/semisynthetic polymers or inorganic particles. Biodegradability is another essential property of hydrogel materials for biomedical application, such as tissue regeneration, as cells need space to grow, migrate, and proliferate [6]. It refers to the capacity of a substance to break down after interactions with biological elements [7]. Most of the hydrogels prepared from natural polymers can be decomposed under the action of enzymes, allowing cells to spread and reshape their surroundings. The rate of biodegradation is another required factor, which depends on properties such as molecular weight and the amorphous or crystalline and hydrophilic/hydrophobic behaviors of polymers [8]. This review outlines the current progress on natural polymer-based hydrogels in biomedical fields. The most widely used natural polymers such as collagen, gelatin, alginate, cellulose, chitosan, and hyaluronic acid are described (Table 1), and natural polymer-based hydrogels including hydrogels prepared from natural polymers, natural/synthetic polymer, and natural/inorganic particles are summarized. Then, the biomedicine applications of natural polymer-based hydrogels in drug delivery, wound healing, and regenerative medicine are summarized and discussed, respectively. fetched_contents.text: Recent Advances in Poly(vinyl alcohol)-Based Hydrogels Abstract Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) is a versatile synthetic polymer, used for the design of hydrogels, porous membranes and films. Its solubility in water, film- and hydrogel-forming capabilities, non-toxicity, crystallinity and excellent mechanical properties, chemical inertness and stability towards biological fluids, superior oxygen and gas barrier properties, good printability and availability (relatively low production cost) are the main aspects that make PVA suitable for a variety of applications, from biomedical and pharmaceutical uses to sensing devices, packaging materials or wastewater treatment. However, pure PVA materials present low stability in water, limited flexibility and poor biocompatibility and biodegradability, which restrict its use alone in various applications. PVA mixed with other synthetic polymers or biomolecules (polysaccharides, proteins, peptides, amino acids etc.), as well as with inorganic/organic compounds, generates a wide variety of materials in which PVA’s shortcomings are considerably improved, and new functionalities are obtained. Also, PVA’s chemical transformation brings new features and opens the door for new and unexpected uses. The present review is focused on recent advances in PVA-based hydrogels. Keywords: poly(vinyl alcohol), hydrogel, wound dressings, tissue engineering, strain sensors 1. Introduction Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) is one of the most important water-soluble synthetic polymers, being inexpensive, non-toxic, readily biodegradable and able to form environment-friendly hydrogels, films and membranes. During the last few years, significant advances were registered in the design of PVA-based materials from new and improved preparation and characterization procedures to testing methods for various and possible unique uses. The high interest for PVA-based hydrogels is reflected by a continuously increasing number of original papers and reviews reported during the last few years (Figure 1). A large number of PVA-based hydrogels are suitable for biomedical and engineering applications, tissue engineering scaffolds, drug delivery, cell culture, implanted artificial muscles and organs, sensors, wound dressings, soft robotics, food packaging or environmental applications. The properties and functions required for a particular application can be fine-tuned by a careful selection of the crosslinking method, PVA characteristics and of other used components for preparing high-performance composites [2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10]. This review is focused mainly on the trends regarding PVA hydrogels as presented in recent studies and some perspectives for future research. 2. Structure and Properties of PVA PVA is produced at an industrial scale through the hydrolysis of poly(vinyl acetate); thus, different degrees of hydrolysis (DHs) (also denoted as the degree of saponification) can be achieved. The corresponding monomer, vinyl alcohol, is thermodynamically unstable and spontaneously transforms into its enol form of acetaldehyde, so the direct polymerization of vinyl alcohol is not possible. PVA samples of different DHs and molecular weights are available on the market [11]. In terms of DHs, PVA samples can be classified as fully hydrolyzed (DH ≥ 97.5%) or partially hydrolyzed (DH < 97.5%), the last category being a copolymer structure, poly(vinyl alcohol-co-vinyl acetate) [12] (Scheme 1); these characteristics influence the overal properties [13]. Thus, the polymer’s solubility in water improves with increasing DH only up to DH = 91% [12]. Fully hydrolyzed PVA samples present good stability at room temperature and are dissolved by water and its mixtures with organic solvents, such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), dimethylformamide (DMF) or N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), by heating at high temperatures (above 80 °C) for several tens of minutes when the strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds are broken [13,14,15]. Water behaves as a marginal solvent for PVA; in aqueous solution, A2 is about 1.4 × 10−4 mol/(cm3g2), whereas NMP or DMSO appear as good solvents, A2 > 2 × 10−3 mol/(cm3g2) when the polymer coil exhibits an extended conformation [16]. Due to the presence of hydrophobic acetate groups, partially hydrolyzed PVA chains are less soluble in polar solvents, when, according to molecular dynamic simulation, the polymer/solvent’s thermodynamic affinity and the surface energy are lower [17]. The solution state (diluted, semidiluted, concentrated, entangled or non-entangled) and intermolecular interactions depend on temperature, concentration and molecular weight [18,19] and dictate the viscosity and viscoelasticity of aqueous solutions, influencing the manufacturing of PVA hydrogels [18]. Below a critical reduced concentration value, (c × [η])cr (where c × [η] is a dimensionless parameter defined as concentration × intrinsic viscosity), the network formation cannot take place; only isolated droplets are generated. The parameter (c × [η])cr is about 2 for PVA in water [18] and indicates the macroscopic percolation transition limit. Above (c × [η])cr, the overlapping between the macromolecular coils determines a phase separation, when a polymer-rich phase is formed and gelation occurs [18,20]. The use of freshly prepared solutions is recommended for preparing hydrogels; otherwise, the prolonged storage of PVA solutions causes the appearance of aggregates; furthermore, several species of microorganisms can degrade the polymer [21]. fetched_contents.text: State of the Art of Hydrogel Wound Dressings Developed by Ionizing Radiation Abstract The development of an ideal hydrogel wound dressing with excellent characteristics is currently a significant demand in wound therapy. The ideal hydrogel wound dressing must provide a moist environment between the wound and the dressing, promote wound healing, absorb excess exudate and toxins, be completely sterile, and not adhere to the wound. The evolution and current status of research on hydrogel wound dressings obtained exclusively through production by ionizing radiation are discussed in this paper review, along with the preparation methods, properties, standard characterization techniques, and their applications in wound dressing. First, we described the methods for synthesizing hydrogel wound dressings with ionizing radiation. Then, standard methods of characterization of hydrogel wound dressings such as gel fraction, swelling degree, sol–gel analysis, rheological properties, morphology, moisture retention capability, and water vapor transmission rate have been investigated. In the end, specific attention was paid to the drug release, antibacterial performance, and cytotoxicity of hydrogels. Moreover, the application of hydrogel in regenerative medicine as wound healing dressing was covered. Keywords: hydrogel, ionizing radiation, wound dressings, crosslinking, healing 1. Introduction The largest organ of the human body is the skin, which represents the main defence barrier against various pathogens commonly encountered in the environment. Wounds on the skin break these barriers and form entry gates for external pathogens [1]. To overcome the exposure of the wounds to the external environment, it is recommended to immediately cover them with suitable dressings depending on the severity of the wound. Mini-report on polymer composition differences

Natural hydrogel dressings are typically based on biologically derived polymers, while synthetic hydrogel dressings rely on chemically engineered polymers. The natural class includes cellulose, chitosan, collagen/gelatin, alginate, hyaluronic acid, starch, guar gum, agarose, and dextran [N1-F1]. The synthetic class includes poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), polyvinyl pyrrolidone, polyethylene oxide, and other synthetic hydrophilic polymers such as PEG and PVA-related materials [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R3]. A review explicitly notes that natural polymers are formed from photosynthesis or biochemical reactions in the natural world, whereas synthetic polymers are chemically engineered [N1-F1]. This source-material distinction directly influences polymer chemistry: natural polymers often retain native functional groups and reactive moieties that can be modified or crosslinked, while synthetic polymers are usually designed for controlled hydrophilicity, solubility, and crosslinking behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Source material also shapes crosslinking strategies. Natural polymers are often crosslinked through chemical means such as covalent bonds, ionic bonds, or physical crosslinking via hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, or physical entanglement [N1-F1]. The review notes that natural polymer-based hydrogels can be fabricated using novel strategies such as dual-cross-linking, microfluidic chip, micropatterning, and 3D/4D bioprinting, which indicates that the source material’s inherent structure and reactivity can be tailored through advanced fabrication methods [N1-F1]. In contrast, synthetic polymers such as PVA are often crosslinked by irradiation, free radical polymerization, or chemical crosslinking, and their crosslinking behavior is highly dependent on molecular weight, degree of hydrolysis, and the specific polymer chemistry [N2-F2]. The PVA review states that PVA is produced through hydrolysis of poly(vinyl acetate), and different degrees of hydrolysis (DH) affect solubility, stability, and the ability to form networks [N2-F2].

Common functional groups and reactive moieties differ between the two classes. Natural polymers tend to contain hydrophilic functional groups derived from their biological origin, such as hydroxyl groups in cellulose, amino groups in chitosan, and carboxyl groups in alginate [N1-F1]. These groups contribute to biocompatibility, swelling, and crosslinking potential [N1-F1]. Synthetic polymers often have more uniform functional groups tailored for hydrophilicity, solubility, and crosslinking. PVA, for example, contains hydroxyl groups and acetate groups depending on the degree of hydrolysis, with partially hydrolyzed PVA having lower solubility and different intermolecular interactions than fully hydrolyzed PVA [N2-F2]. PEG and PVP are similarly characterized by hydrophilic functional groups that make them useful in hydrogel formation [N2-R3][N2-R2].

Overall, natural hydrogels are defined by their biological source and native chemistry, while synthetic hydrogels are defined by chemical engineering and tunable polymer design. Both classes can be crosslinked chemically or physically, but the source-material basis determines the starting functional groups, the types of crosslinkable moieties, and the overall polymer chemistry [N1-F1][N2-F2][N2-R2].

Mini-report on structural and physical differences

Porosity, crosslinking, and network density differ substantially between natural and synthetic hydrogel dressings. Natural hydrogels are often described as having a structure that can mimic the extracellular matrix and provide a humid, protective barrier, while synthetic hydrogels are more commonly engineered for controlled network density and mechanical behavior [N3-R2][N3-F3]. The structural evidence indicates that crosslinking density and network formation are central to hydrogel properties, with higher crosslinking density typically associated with more stable but stiffer networks [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The review on ionizing radiation crosslinking notes that hydrogel synthesis can use physical crosslinking through ionic interactions, hydrogen bonds, crystallization, hydrophobic interaction, or protein interaction, and chemical crosslinking through free radical polymerization or enzymatic reaction [N3-F3]. In contrast, synthetic PVA-based hydrogels are formed through hydrolysis of poly(vinyl acetate), and the degree of hydrolysis and molecular weight strongly influence network formation, stability, and phase behavior [N2-F2]. The PVA review also emphasizes that crosslinking method, PVA characteristics, and other components determine the final hydrogel’s performance [N2-F2].

Morphology and swelling behavior are closely linked to wound contact and fluid management. Natural hydrogels are often designed to absorb large amounts of water and retain a moist wound environment, which is essential for wound healing [N3-R1][N3-R5]. The structural evidence states that hydrogels can absorb significant amounts of fluid, swell, and closely mimic the characteristics of living tissue [N3-R5]. The review on ionizing radiation crosslinking explicitly describes swelling as a key property of hydrogel wound dressings, noting that the gel can absorb a large amount of water in the blood [N3-F3]. Synthetic hydrogels similarly depend on swelling behavior, but the PVA review explains that water behaves as a marginal solvent for PVA and that the swelling capacity is influenced by degree of hydrolysis, concentration, and molecular weight [N2-F2]. The network and crosslinking density further determine how much fluid is absorbed and retained, which in turn affects wound exudate management and moisture balance [N3-R4][N3-R3].

Mechanical properties affect handling and performance. Natural hydrogels are often noted for good biocompatibility and flexibility, but they can face limitations such as limited toughness and poor mechanical strength [N1-F1][N4-R1]. The review on natural polymer-based hydrogels states that most natural polymeric hydrogels have limited toughness and poor mechanical properties, and that several efforts are made to improve them through chemical cross-linking, physical cross-linking, and mixing with other synthetic/semisynthetic polymers or inorganic particles [N1-F1]. Synthetic hydrogels, by contrast, can be engineered to have higher mechanical performance. The PVA review highlights that PVA has excellent mechanical properties, good oxygen and gas barrier properties, and superior printability, although pure PVA alone has low stability in water and poor biocompatibility/biodegradability [N2-F2]. The structural evidence also notes that the thermal and shear history influence network formation and mechanical properties of PVA-based materials [N2-F2]. This means that synthetic hydrogels can be tuned for handling and performance, while natural hydrogels often require crosslinking or composite strategies to achieve adequate mechanical behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2].

In summary, natural hydrogels typically have a more biologically inspired structure with variable crosslinking density and swelling behavior, while synthetic hydrogels are more engineering-oriented, with tunable porosity, network density, and mechanical properties. Both classes are important for wound dressings because their structure directly determines how they interact with wound fluid, maintain moisture, and support healing [N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2].

Mini-report on degradation and biocompatibility differences

Biodegradation rates and mechanisms differ between natural and synthetic hydrogels. Natural hydrogels are often designed for controlled degradation, and the review explicitly states that they are derived from natural polymers that can be decomposed under enzyme action, allowing cells to spread and reshape their surroundings [N1-F1]. The degradation review notes that hydrogel degradation can occur through four main mechanisms: solubilization, chemical hydrolysis, enzyme-induced degradation, and other mechanisms such as oxidation and photodegradation [N6-R1][N6-R3]. It also states that the most common bond-breaking mechanisms are hydrolysis, solubilization/ionization, oxidation, photodegradation, and enzymatic degradation [N6-R3]. For synthetic hydrogels, the degradation review similarly describes hydrolysis of either the crosslinks or the polymer backbone as a major degradability mechanism [N6-R2]. The PVA review adds that crosslinked hydrogels tend to induce resistance to degradation and that ester hydrolysis rate constant is higher for crosslinked gels compared to non-crosslinked ones [N6-R5]. This implies that synthetic hydrogels can be more stable or more resistant to degradation, depending on crosslinking and backbone chemistry.

Degradation affects material stability and wound interface behavior. Natural hydrogels are advantageous because their degradation can be enzyme-mediated and compatible with biological environments [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The review on natural polymer-based hydrogels notes that biodegradation is an essential property for tissue regeneration, as cells need space to grow, migrate, and proliferate [N1-F1]. The degradation review further explains that degradation behavior influences the rate at which the material breaks down and whether the wound interface remains stable [N6-R1]. For synthetic hydrogels, the PVA review states that pure PVA has limited flexibility and poor biocompatibility/biodegradability, and that mixing with other polymers or biomolecules can improve biocompatibility [N2-F2]. The crosslinking-related evidence also suggests that higher crosslinking density can increase resistance to degradation [N6-R5]. This means that synthetic hydrogels may degrade more slowly or remain in the wound longer, potentially affecting the interface stability and healing dynamics.

Tradeoffs between biocompatibility, degradation, and long-term performance are evident in both classes. Natural hydrogels are generally more biocompatible because they are derived from natural polymers with intrinsic biocompatibility [N1-F1]. However, they can degrade too rapidly or not quickly enough, depending on the polymer and crosslinking strategy [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The review also notes that natural polymer-based hydrogels face limitations such as low mechanical strength, rapid degradation, source variability, high production costs, and other challenges [N4-R1]. Synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for superior mechanical performance and controlled degradation, but they may have lower intrinsic biocompatibility and may require additional crosslinking or additive strategies to achieve adequate performance [N2-F2][N4-R1]. The degradation review further indicates that crosslinking can alter degradation behavior, with crosslinked gels being more resistant to degradation [N6-R5]. Overall, the tradeoff is that natural hydrogels offer better intrinsic biocompatibility and controlled degradation but may need improvement in mechanical and long-term stability, while synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for better mechanical and degradation performance but may require additional modifications to achieve optimal biocompatibility [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1].

Mini-report on practical implications and comparison

Each class is better suited clinically depending on the desired balance of biocompatibility, degradation, and manufacturability. Natural hydrogels are often preferred when biocompatibility and controlled degradation are priorities. The review states that natural polymer-based hydrogels usually have excellent biocompatibility owing to the intrinsic properties of natural polymers [N1-F1]. They are also well-suited for wound dressings because they can absorb a large volume of water, provide a moist wound environment, and mimic the extracellular matrix [N3-R2][N3-R5]. However, natural hydrogels are limited by low mechanical strength, rapid degradation, source variability, high production costs, and other challenges [N4-R1]. These limitations make them less suitable for applications requiring long-term structural integrity or extreme mechanical performance.

Synthetic hydrogels are often preferred when mechanical performance, manufacturability, and controlled degradation behavior are important. The PVA review highlights that PVA is inexpensive, non-toxic, readily biodegradable, and can be used for a variety of biomedical and engineering applications [N2-F2]. It also notes that PVA can be mixed with other synthetic polymers or biomolecules to improve its shortcomings and obtain new functionalities [N2-F2]. Synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for specific mechanical properties, such as higher toughness, better oxygen and gas barrier properties, and improved printability [N2-F2]. However, they may have lower intrinsic biocompatibility and may require crosslinking or additive strategies to achieve adequate performance [N2-F2][N4-R1]. The degradation review also indicates that crosslinking can increase resistance to degradation, which may be desirable in some clinical settings but less so in others where rapid degradation is needed [N6-R5].

The tradeoffs between biocompatibility, degradation, and manufacturability are central to material choice. Natural hydrogels generally offer better biocompatibility and more favorable degradation behavior for wound healing, but they are harder to manufacture consistently and may require additional processing to improve mechanical properties [N1-F1][N4-R1]. Synthetic hydrogels are easier to manufacture and can be engineered for precise mechanical and degradation profiles, but they may require more extensive modification to achieve adequate biocompatibility [N2-F2][N4-R1]. The degradation review further notes that degradation mechanisms such as hydrolysis, solubilization, and enzymatic degradation influence the material’s stability and wound interface behavior [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Material choice also affects drug delivery and bioactive release. Natural hydrogels are often used in drug delivery because they can be designed to release bioactive molecules in a controlled manner [N1-F1]. The review on natural polymer-based hydrogels mentions that these materials are used as carriers for drug delivery, tissue regeneration, wound healing, and other biomedical applications [N1-F1]. The PVA review notes that PVA-based composite hydrogels can deliver drugs, DNA, growth factors, nanoparticles, and proteins [N2-R4]. Synthetic hydrogels are similarly useful for drug delivery, but the choice of polymer chemistry and crosslinking affects release kinetics and bioactivity [N2-F2]. The crosslinking evidence also indicates that network density and crosslinking strategy influence swelling and diffusion behavior, which in turn governs release [N3-R4][N3-R3]. Overall, the choice between natural and synthetic hydrogels depends on whether the clinical goal is to prioritize biocompatibility and controlled degradation or mechanical performance and manufacturability, and the specific application determines the optimal balance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1].

Overall, the tradeoff is that natural hydrogels offer better intrinsic biocompatibility and controlled degradation but may need improvement in mechanical and long-term stability, while synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for better mechanical and degradation performance but may require additional modifications to achieve optimal biocompatibility [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1].

## 6) Practical implications: where each class is better suited clinically

Each class is better suited clinically depending on the desired balance of biocompatibility, degradation, and manufacturability. Natural hydrogels are often preferred when biocompatibility and controlled degradation are priorities. The review states that natural polymer-based hydrogels usually have excellent biocompatibility owing to the intrinsic properties of natural polymers [N1-F1]. However, natural hydrogels are limited by low mechanical strength, rapid degradation, source variability, high production costs, and other challenges [N4-R1]. These limitations make them less suitable for applications requiring long-term structural integrity or extreme mechanical performance.

Synthetic hydrogels are often preferred when mechanical performance, manufacturability, and controlled degradation behavior are important. The PVA review highlights that PVA is inexpensive, non-toxic, readily biodegradable, and can be used for a variety of biomedical and engineering applications [N2-F2]. It also notes that PVA can be mixed with other synthetic polymers or biomolecules to improve its shortcomings and obtain new functionalities [N2-F2]. Synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for specific mechanical properties, such as higher toughness, better oxygen and gas barrier properties, and improved printability [N2-F2]. However, they may have lower intrinsic biocompatibility and may require crosslinking or additive strategies to achieve adequate performance [N2-F2][N4-R1]. The degradation review also indicates that crosslinking can increase resistance to degradation, which may be desirable in some clinical settings but less so in others where rapid degradation is needed [N6-R5].

## 7) Tradeoffs and drug delivery relevance

The tradeoffs between biocompatibility, degradation, and manufacturability are central to material choice. Natural hydrogels generally offer better biocompatibility and more favorable degradation behavior for wound healing, but they are harder to manufacture consistently and may require additional processing to improve mechanical properties [N1-F1][N4-R1]. Synthetic hydrogels are easier to manufacture and can be engineered for precise mechanical and degradation profiles, but they may require more extensive modification to achieve adequate biocompatibility [N2-F2][N4-R1]. The degradation review further notes that degradation mechanisms such as hydrolysis, solubilization, and enzymatic degradation influence the material’s stability and wound interface behavior [N6-R1][N6-R3].

## Bottom line

In short, natural and synthetic hydrogel dressings differ primarily in their polymer sources and resulting chemistry: natural hydrogels are derived from biological polymers with native functional groups and often biologically inspired crosslinking, while synthetic hydrogels are chemically engineered with tunable hydrophilicity and crosslinking behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Structurally, natural hydrogels often mimic the extracellular matrix and are designed for swelling and moisture retention, while synthetic hydrogels are engineered for controlled network density, mechanical performance, and specific degradation behavior [N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2]. Biocompatibility is generally stronger in natural hydrogels, but synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for better mechanical and degradation performance at the cost of sometimes requiring additional biocompatibility modifications [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1]. Mini-report on polymer composition differences

Natural hydrogel dressings are typically based on biologically derived polymers, while synthetic hydrogel dressings rely on chemically engineered polymers. The natural class includes cellulose, chitosan, collagen/gelatin, alginate, hyaluronic acid, starch, guar gum, agarose, and dextran [N1-F1]. The synthetic class includes poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), polyvinyl pyrrolidone, polyethylene oxide, and other synthetic hydrophilic polymers such as PEG and PVA-related materials [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R3]. A review explicitly notes that natural polymers are formed from photosynthesis or biochemical reactions in the natural world, whereas synthetic polymers are chemically engineered [N1-F1]. This source-material distinction directly influences polymer chemistry: natural polymers often retain native functional groups and reactive moieties that can be modified or crosslinked, while synthetic polymers are usually designed for controlled hydrophilicity, solubility, and crosslinking behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Source material also shapes crosslinking strategies. Natural polymers are often crosslinked through chemical means such as covalent bonds, ionic bonds, or physical crosslinking via hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, or physical entanglement [N1-F1]. The review notes that natural polymer-based hydrogels can be fabricated using novel strategies such as dual-cross-linking, microfluidic chip, micropatterning, and 3D/4D bioprinting, which indicates that the source material’s inherent structure and reactivity can be tailored through advanced fabrication methods [N1-F1]. In contrast, synthetic polymers such as PVA are often crosslinked by irradiation, free radical polymerization, or chemical crosslinking, and their crosslinking behavior is highly dependent on molecular weight, degree of hydrolysis, and the specific polymer chemistry [N2-F2]. The PVA review states that PVA is produced through hydrolysis of poly(vinyl acetate), and different degrees of hydrolysis (DH) affect solubility, stability, and the ability to form networks [N2-F2].

Common functional groups and reactive moieties differ between the two classes. Natural polymers tend to contain hydrophilic functional groups derived from their biological origin, such as hydroxyl groups in cellulose, amino groups in chitosan, and carboxyl groups in alginate [N1-F1]. These groups contribute to biocompatibility, swelling, and crosslinking potential [N1-F1]. Synthetic polymers often have more uniform functional groups tailored for hydrophilicity, solubility, and crosslinking. PVA, for example, contains hydroxyl groups and acetate groups depending on the degree of hydrolysis, with partially hydrolyzed PVA having lower solubility and different intermolecular interactions than fully hydrolyzed PVA [N2-F2]. PEG and PVP are similarly characterized by hydrophilic functional groups that make them useful in hydrogel formation [N2-R3][N2-R2].

Overall, natural hydrogels are defined by their biological source and native chemistry, while synthetic hydrogels are defined by chemical engineering and tunable polymer design. Both classes can be crosslinked chemically or physically, but the source-material basis determines the starting functional groups, the types of crosslinkable moieties, and the overall polymer chemistry [N1-F1][N2-F2][N2-R2].

Mechanical properties affect handling and performance. Natural hydrogels are often noted for good biocompatibility and flexibility, but they can face limitations such as limited toughness and poor mechanical strength [N1-F1][N4-R1]. The review on natural polymer-based hydrogels states that most natural polymeric hydrogels have limited toughness and poor mechanical properties, and that several efforts are made to improve them through chemical cross-linking, physical cross-linking, and mixing with other synthetic/semisynthetic polymers or inorganic particles [N1-F1]. This means that synthetic hydrogels can be tuned for handling and performance, while natural hydrogels often require crosslinking or composite strategies to achieve adequate mechanical behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2].

In summary, natural hydrogels typically have a more biologically inspired structure with variable crosslinking density and swelling behavior, while synthetic hydrogels are more engineering-oriented, with tunable porosity, network density, and mechanical properties. ## 1) Polymer composition: the main difference is source and chemistry

The central distinction between natural and synthetic hydrogel dressings lies in their polymer sources and the resulting chemistry. Natural hydrogel dressings are typically based on biologically derived polymers, such as cellulose, chitosan, collagen/gelatin, alginate, hyaluronic acid, starch, guar gum, agarose, and dextran [N1-F1]. These polymers are formed from photosynthesis or biochemical reactions in the natural world, which gives them an inherent biological origin and often a native chemistry that includes hydrophilic functional groups and reactive moieties [N1-F1]. In contrast, synthetic hydrogel dressings rely on chemically engineered polymers, including poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), polyvinyl pyrrolidone, polyethylene oxide, and other synthetic hydrophilic polymers such as PEG and PVA-related materials [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R3]. A review explicitly notes that natural polymers are formed from natural processes, while synthetic polymers are chemically engineered [N1-F1].

This source-material distinction directly affects polymer chemistry and crosslinking. Natural polymers often retain native functional groups and reactive moieties that can be modified or crosslinked, while synthetic polymers are usually designed for controlled hydrophilicity, solubility, and crosslinking behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Source material also shapes crosslinking strategies: natural polymers are often crosslinked through chemical means such as covalent bonds, ionic bonds, or physical crosslinking via hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, or physical entanglement [N1-F1]. The review also notes that natural polymer-based hydrogels can be fabricated using novel strategies such as dual-cross-linking, microfluidic chip, micropatterning, and 3D/4D bioprinting, indicating that the source material’s inherent structure and reactivity can be tailored through advanced fabrication methods [N1-F1]. In contrast, synthetic polymers such as PVA are often crosslinked by irradiation, free radical polymerization, or chemical crosslinking, and their crosslinking behavior is highly dependent on molecular weight, degree of hydrolysis, and the specific polymer chemistry [N2-F2]. The PVA review states that PVA is produced through hydrolysis of poly(vinyl acetate), and different degrees of hydrolysis (DH) affect solubility, stability, and the ability to form networks [N2-F2].

Common functional groups and reactive moieties differ between the two classes. Natural polymers tend to contain hydrophilic functional groups derived from their biological origin, such as hydroxyl groups in cellulose, amino groups in chitosan, and carboxyl groups in alginate [N1-F1]. These groups contribute to biocompatibility, swelling, and crosslinking potential [N1-F1]. Synthetic polymers often have more uniform functional groups tailored for hydrophilicity, solubility, and crosslinking. PVA, for example, contains hydroxyl groups and acetate groups depending on the degree of hydrolysis, with partially hydrolyzed PVA having lower solubility and different intermolecular interactions than fully hydrolyzed PVA [N2-F2]. PEG and PVP are similarly characterized by hydrophilic functional groups that make them useful in hydrogel formation [N2-R3][N2-R2].

## 2) Structural characteristics: porosity, crosslinking, and network density

Porosity, crosslinking, and network density differ substantially between natural and synthetic hydrogel dressings. Natural hydrogels are often described as having a structure that can mimic the extracellular matrix and provide a humid, protective barrier, while synthetic hydrogels are more commonly engineered for controlled network density and mechanical behavior [N3-R2][N3-F3]. The structural evidence indicates that crosslinking density and network formation are central to hydrogel properties, with higher crosslinking density typically associated with more stable but stiffer networks [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The review on ionizing radiation crosslinking notes that hydrogel synthesis can use physical crosslinking through ionic interactions, hydrogen bonds, crystallization, hydrophobic interaction, or protein interaction, and chemical crosslinking through free radical polymerization or enzymatic reaction [N3-F3]. In contrast, synthetic PVA-based hydrogels are formed through hydrolysis of poly(vinyl acetate), and the degree of hydrolysis and molecular weight strongly influence network formation, stability, and phase behavior [N2-F2]. The PVA review also emphasizes that crosslinking method, PVA characteristics, and other components determine the final hydrogel’s performance [N2-F2].

## 3) Morphology and swelling behavior: wound contact and fluid management

Morphology and swelling behavior are closely linked to wound contact and fluid management. Natural hydrogels are often designed to absorb large amounts of water and retain a moist wound environment, which is essential for wound healing [N3-R1][N3-R5]. The structural evidence states that hydrogels can absorb significant amounts of fluid, swell, and closely mimic the characteristics of living tissue [N3-R5]. The review on ionizing radiation crosslinking explicitly describes swelling as a key property of hydrogel wound dressings, noting that the gel can absorb a large amount of water in the blood [N3-F3]. Synthetic hydrogels similarly depend on swelling behavior, but the PVA review explains that water behaves as a marginal solvent for PVA and that the swelling capacity is influenced by degree of hydrolysis, concentration, and molecular weight [N2-F2]. The network and crosslinking density further determine how much fluid is absorbed and retained, which in turn affects wound exudate management and moisture balance [N3-R4][N3-R3].

## 4) Mechanical properties: handling and performance

Mechanical properties affect handling and performance. Natural hydrogels are often noted for good biocompatibility and flexibility, but they can face limitations such as limited toughness and poor mechanical strength [N1-F1][N4-R1]. The review on natural polymer-based hydrogels states that most natural polymeric hydrogels have limited toughness and poor mechanical properties, and that several efforts are made to improve them through chemical cross-linking, physical cross-linking, and mixing with other synthetic/semisynthetic polymers or inorganic particles [N1-F1]. Synthetic hydrogels, by contrast, can be engineered to have higher mechanical performance. The PVA review highlights that PVA has excellent mechanical properties, good oxygen and gas barrier properties, and superior printability, although pure PVA alone has low stability in water and poor biocompatibility/biodegradability [N2-F2]. The structural evidence also notes that the thermal and shear history influence network formation and mechanical properties of PVA-based materials [N2-F2]. This means that synthetic hydrogels can be tuned for handling and performance, while natural hydrogels often require crosslinking or composite strategies to achieve adequate mechanical behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 5) Degradation and biocompatibility: another major distinction

Biodegradation rates and mechanisms differ between natural and synthetic hydrogels. Natural hydrogels are often designed for controlled degradation, and the review explicitly states that they are derived from natural polymers that can be decomposed under enzyme action, allowing cells to spread and reshape their surroundings [N1-F1]. The PVA review adds that crosslinked hydrogels tend to induce resistance to degradation and that ester hydrolysis rate constant is higher for crosslinked gels compared to non-crosslinked ones [N6-R5]. This implies that synthetic hydrogels can be more stable or more resistant to degradation, depending on crosslinking and backbone chemistry.

The crosslinking-related evidence also suggests that higher crosslinking density can increase resistance to degradation [N6-R5]. This means that synthetic hydrogels may degrade more slowly or remain in the wound longer, potentially affecting the interface stability and healing dynamics.

The tradeoffs between biocompatibility, degradation, and long-term performance are evident in both classes. Natural hydrogels are generally more biocompatible because they are derived from natural polymers with intrinsic biocompatibility [N1-F1]. However, they can degrade too rapidly or not quickly enough, depending on the polymer and crosslinking strategy [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The degradation review further indicates that crosslinking can alter degradation behavior, with crosslinked gels being more resistant to degradation [N6-R5]. Overall, the tradeoff is that natural hydrogels offer better intrinsic biocompatibility and controlled degradation but may need improvement in mechanical and long-term stability, while synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for better mechanical and degradation performance but may require additional modifications to achieve optimal biocompatibility [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1].

## 6) Practical implications: where each class is better suited clinically

Each class is better suited clinically depending on the desired balance of biocompatibility, degradation, and manufacturability. Natural hydrogels are often preferred when biocompatibility and controlled degradation are priorities. The review states that natural polymer-based hydrogels usually have excellent biocompatibility owing to the intrinsic properties of natural polymers [N1-F1]. Synthetic hydrogels are often preferred when mechanical performance, manufacturability, and controlled degradation behavior are important. It also notes that PVA can be mixed with other synthetic polymers or biomolecules to improve its shortcomings and obtain new functionalities [N2-F2]. The degradation review also indicates that crosslinking can increase resistance to degradation, which may be desirable in some clinical settings but less so in others where rapid degradation is needed [N6-R5].

## 7) Tradeoffs and drug delivery relevance

The tradeoffs between biocompatibility, degradation, and manufacturability are central to material choice. Natural hydrogels generally offer better biocompatibility and more favorable degradation behavior for wound healing, but they are harder to manufacture consistently and may require additional processing to improve mechanical properties [N1-F1][N4-R1]. Synthetic hydrogels are easier to manufacture and can be engineered for precise mechanical and degradation profiles, but they may require more extensive modification to achieve adequate biocompatibility [N2-F2][N4-R1]. The degradation review further notes that degradation mechanisms such as hydrolysis, solubilization, and enzymatic degradation influence the material’s stability and wound interface behavior [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Material choice also affects drug delivery and bioactive release. The review on natural polymer-based hydrogels mentions that these materials are used as carriers for drug delivery, tissue regeneration, wound healing, and other biomedical applications [N1-F1]. The crosslinking evidence also indicates that network density and crosslinking strategy influence swelling and diffusion behavior, which in turn governs release [N3-R4][N3-R3]. Overall, the choice between natural and synthetic hydrogels depends on whether the clinical goal is to prioritize biocompatibility and controlled degradation or mechanical performance and manufacturability, and the specific application determines the optimal balance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1].

## Bottom line

In short, natural and synthetic hydrogel dressings differ primarily in their polymer sources and resulting chemistry: natural hydrogels are derived from biological polymers with native functional groups and often biologically inspired crosslinking, while synthetic hydrogels are chemically engineered with tunable hydrophilicity and crosslinking behavior [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Structurally, natural hydrogels often mimic the extracellular matrix and are designed for swelling and moisture retention, while synthetic hydrogels are engineered for controlled network density, mechanical performance, and specific degradation behavior [N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2]. Biocompatibility is generally stronger in natural hydrogels, but synthetic hydrogels can be engineered for better mechanical and degradation performance at the cost of sometimes requiring additional biocompatibility modifications [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1]. Clinically, the best choice depends on whether the application needs superior biocompatibility and controlled degradation, superior mechanical performance and manufacturability, or a balance of both, with material choice also affecting drug delivery and bioactive release [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R1][N2-R4].
